newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy begins second round of welfare talks.
newsitem.headline: Italy begins second round of welfare talks.

text.p: The Italian government on Wednesday opened a second round of talks with union leaders and employers on welfare reform after a shaky start a month ago.

Italy is under pressure to carry out a convincing reform of social spending and to shake up its pensions system to prove that public finances will be kept under control before the planned 1999 launch of the single European currency.

The second round was concentrating on how to reduce tax evasion and tackle unemployment through proposals to encourage part-time work, reduce the average work week and create jobs in the poorer south.

"There is a common interest to verify what are the best times and ways to implement these measures in everyone's interest," Labour minister Tiziano Treu said in a radio interview on Wednesday morning before the talks began.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi opened the talks last month with the three main union confederations, trade bodies and employers' group Confindustria.
But the government immediately ran into trouble with the unions over the thorny question of how to review the country's generous early retirement system.
The system allows Italians to draw a pension based on the length of service even before they have reach mandatory retirement age.

Trade unions agree that the welfare system should be changed, but they want reforms to focus on providing employment and unemployment benefits. They are staunchly against cuts in spending, especially for pensions.

"Providing a serious response on employment, training and taxes, which are particularly dear to the unions, it will be easier to then make sacrifices." Treu told Milan's Corriere della Sera newspaper on Wednesday.
Treu added, however, that "this does not mean there will be cuts to pensions."
Pension reform is on the agenda for July 15, according to the government's timetable for the meetings.

During Wednesday's talks, the parties were due to discuss how to implement measures included in an employment law passed by Parliament last month and a labour pact signed by the government and unions last summer.
The law sets aside 400 billion lire ($235 million) for incentives to provide part-time employment and reduced working weeks. It also aims to provide 100,000 jobs in southern Italy.
The labour pact includes plans for public works projects that will also provide new jobs throughout the country.
The unions also have called for a rigorous commitment by the government to curb the country's high level of tax evasion which they say promotes a hidden economy and drains revenue from the state.
The discussion groups are expected to produce initial findings by the end of July
